name: Tuvalu
summary: No official Tuvaluan procedure for bringing a casket into Tuvalu was found. Plan for an embalmed body in a sealed casket with a certified death certificate, travelling via Fiji (Nadi), and confirm the file with the Tuvalu Ministry of Health and the airline before departure.
documents: Certified death certificate or medical certificate of cause of death, in English (not confirmed by Tuvaluan sources)
Medical letter that the death was not due to an infectious disease (usual regional practice; not confirmed)
Embalming certificate and casket sealing certificate from the funeral home (not confirmed)
Copy of the deceased's passport
Fiji Ministry of Health transit clearance if the casket transits Nadi
coffin: Not published by Tuvaluan authorities. An embalmed body in a hermetically sealed casket inside an outer case is the safe assumption; confirm with the Ministry of Health.
embalming: Not specified in any official Tuvaluan source found. Embalming is in practice needed for the long routing via Fiji and is required by Fiji for remains passing through Nadi.
consular: Tuvalu has very few diplomatic missions (High Commission in Suva, Fiji). No published consular transfer permit was found; ask the Tuvalu High Commission in Suva or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Funafuti.
arrival: Arrival at Funafuti International Airport. Health and customs clearance procedures for remains are not published. The family or a local undertaker collects the casket; there is no funeral industry infrastructure to speak of, so burial usually follows quickly.
private_aviation: Funafuti is the only international airport, served by scheduled flights from Suva. A private aircraft needs a landing permit from Tuvaluan civil aviation and customs and health officers present on arrival; long over-water sectors limit aircraft choice. No rule specific to human remains on private flights was found.
private_jet_note: Obtain landing clearance for Funafuti and the Ministry of Health's written agreement before take-off.
export: No official information found on permits for removing a body from Tuvalu. Expect a medical cause-of-death certificate from Princess Margaret Hospital, death registration, and police involvement for unnatural deaths. Embalming facilities are very limited locally, which constrains delays.
export_points: No published export procedure; ask the Ministry of Health
Embalming capacity on Funafuti is very limited
Transit via Fiji needs Fiji Ministry of Health approval

name: Nauru
summary: Nauru has a Funeral, Burial and Cremation Act 2017 (with sections on disposal within 24 hours and removal of remains from the Republic), but its text could not be opened and no official procedure for incoming caskets was found. Confirm requirements with the Nauru Department of Health before departure.
documents: Certified death certificate stating the cause of death, in English (not confirmed)
Medical letter that the death was not due to an infectious disease (not confirmed)
Embalming and casket sealing certificates (not confirmed)
Copy of the deceased's passport
coffin: Not published. A sealed casket with an embalmed body is the safe assumption; confirm with the Department of Health.
embalming: Not confirmed by an official source. Embalming should be expected given the long routing via Brisbane or Fiji.
consular: Nauru has few missions abroad (e.g. a High Commission in Suva, a Consulate in Brisbane). No published consular transfer permit was found; ask the nearest Nauruan mission.
arrival: Arrival at Nauru International Airport. The 2017 Act reportedly provides for disposal of remains within 24 hours, which may apply after arrival; this could not be verified. Customs and health clearance steps are not published.
private_aviation: Nauru International Airport is the only airport, served mainly by Nauru Airlines. Private aircraft need prior landing permission and Nauru's entry rules for accompanying passengers (visa required for most nationals). No rule specific to human remains on private flights was found.
private_jet_note: Secure landing permission and visas for escorts before take-off; burial may be expected within 24 hours of arrival.
export: The Funeral, Burial and Cremation Act 2017 contains a section on removal of human remains from the Republic, but its conditions could not be verified. Expect a medical cause-of-death certificate from RON Hospital, death registration and Department of Health approval.

name: Cook Islands
summary: Under the Public Health Act 2004, remains brought into the Cook Islands for burial or cremation must be kept embalmed and in a sealed, impervious container, and must be buried or cremated within 48 hours of arrival unless the Secretary of Health grants a written exemption.
documents: Certified death certificate stating the cause of death, in English (expected; not listed in the Act)
Embalming certificate (embalming is legally required)
Casket sealing certificate from the funeral director (expected)
Written exemption from the Secretary of Health if burial cannot take place within 48 hours of arrival
Copy of the deceased's passport
coffin: Section 44 of the Public Health Act 2004: remains must be kept encased in a sealed and impervious container at all times while held or transported in the Cook Islands. Land burial must be in a sealed and impervious crypt (section 46). Who witnesses the sealing is not specified.
embalming: Required by law: remains brought in must be kept embalmed until burial or cremation (section 44).
consular: No consular transfer permit is set out in the Act. Most repatriations come from New Zealand (Cook Islanders are NZ citizens); the Cook Islands High Commission in Wellington and Consulate in Auckland can advise.
arrival: Burial or cremation must take place within 48 hours of the remains being brought into the Cook Islands (section 44), unless the Secretary of Health issues a written exemption with conditions (section 45). Where infection with a notifiable condition is suspected, the medical officer may direct special handling (section 86). The family or funeral director collects at Rarotonga.
private_aviation: Rarotonga International Airport is the port of entry. No rule specific to private flights carrying remains was found; the 48-hour burial clock starts when the remains are brought into the country, so the funeral must be ready before landing. Remains for burial on an outer island must be embalmed, sealed and buried within 48 hours of receipt (section 43).
private_jet_note: Burial within 48 hours of arrival is a legal requirement; have the funeral ready before take-off.
export: Remains received in the Cook Islands to be buried elsewhere must be embalmed and sealed within 24 hours and transported out of the Cook Islands within 48 hours of receipt (section 43), unless the Secretary of Health grants an exemption. Embalming capacity is limited; flights to Auckland are the usual route.
export_points: Embalm and seal within 24 hours of receipt
Remains must leave the Cook Islands within 48 hours
Exemptions only by written decision of the Secretary of Health
Coroner may be involved under the Coroners Act

at_a_glance.consular: No consular permit in the law

key_points: Embalming and a sealed casket are legal requirements

name: Wallis and Futuna
summary: A French overseas collectivity: a body coming from abroad travels with the French consulate's body transport authorisation, in a sealed casket. Local rules specific to Wallis and Futuna are not published; confirm with the Agence de santé and the Administrateur supérieur.
documents: Death certificate (acte de deces)
Body transport authorisation issued by the French embassy or consulate in the country of death
Certificate of no contagious disease (French practice; confirm locally)
Casket closing record (French practice; confirm locally)
Identity document of the deceased
coffin: French practice for international transport is a hermetically sealed, zinc-lined casket. No Wallis and Futuna specific rule was found; confirm locally.
embalming: Not specified in a Wallis and Futuna source. French practice generally expects conservation care for long-distance transport; confirm with the funeral operator.
consular: For a death abroad, the French embassy or consulate issues an authorisation to transport the body or ashes for repatriation. Transcription of the death into French civil records is recommended but not mandatory.
arrival: Arrival at Wallis-Hihifo airport, usually via Noumea (Aircalin). Remains for Futuna are then flown on to Futuna. Transfers from mainland France usually transit Japan and New Caledonia. A State aid (law of 28 February 2017) and a separate territorial aid can cover part of the air transport cost under conditions.
private_aviation: Wallis-Hihifo is the international airport; Futuna (Vele) is a short domestic strip. A private flight avoids the transit problems of scheduled routings (Japan, New Caledonia), but needs French overseas landing and customs arrangements. No rule specific to human remains on private flights was found.
private_jet_note: Plan clearance at Wallis-Hihifo; Futuna's strip suits only small aircraft.
export: Not published for Wallis and Futuna. Expect a death certificate, a medical certificate, and authorisation from the territorial administration (Administrateur superieur) and health agency; routing to France goes via New Caledonia. Confirm with the Agence de sante.
export_points: Local procedure not published; ask the Agence de sante
Usual routing via Noumea
State and territorial aid may cover part of transport costs

name: Northern Mariana Islands
summary: A US territory: remains arriving from abroad fall under US federal (CDC) import rules, which apply to the Northern Mariana Islands. Non-cremated remains must be in a leak-proof container and, unless embalmed, travel with a death certificate stating the cause of death.
documents: Death certificate stating the cause of death, with English translation if needed (required unless embalmed)
Consular mortuary certificate and transit permit from the US embassy or consulate when there is no death certificate (for US citizens)
Embalming certificate if embalmed
CDC import permit only if the death involved an infectious agent and the body is not embalmed
Burial-transit permit from the US state of death for domestic shipments (local CNMI requirement not verified)
coffin: Federal rule: remains must be fully contained in a leak-proof container (double-layered puncture-resistant body bag, casket with certified leak-proof lining, or sealed metal transfer case). Hermetic sealing is not a federal requirement; airlines may require it.
embalming: Not required by federal rules. Embalmed remains need no CDC permit; unembalmed remains need a death certificate or importer certification.
consular: For US citizens who die abroad, the US embassy or consulate issues the consular report of death and mortuary documents. No CNMI-specific consular step.
arrival: Remains must go directly to a licensed mortuary, cemetery or crematory. Local customs clearance applies (CNMI is outside the US customs territory). Death records are held by the Commonwealth Healthcare Corporation Health and Vital Statistics Office.
pouch: Federal rules accept a double-layered, puncture-resistant, leak-proof body bag; airline and local funeral home acceptance must be confirmed.
private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights carrying remains was found. A private aircraft arriving from abroad must land at an airport with customs (Saipan) and the remains must meet CDC rules on arrival.
private_jet_note: Arrive at Saipan with the death certificate and a receiving licensed funeral home arranged.
export: Local procedure not verified. Expect a death certificate from the Commonwealth Healthcare Corporation, a burial-transit permit and embalming by a local funeral home; the destination country's rules apply.
export_points: Death certificate via CHCC Health and Vital Statistics Office
Local burial-transit permit procedure not verified
Check the destination country's requirements

at_a_glance.arrival: Directly to a licensed funeral home
